(a) Let there be L sites in each direction, with periodic boundary conditions and lattice spacing a. The allowed dimensionless lattice momenta are q_i = 2π n_i/L, with n_i = 0,...,L−1 (understood modulo L). A complete one-particle basis is |q,f,s⟩ = a†_{qfs}|0⟩, where f = n,p and s = ↑,↓. For example, n†_{qs} = L^(−3/2) Σ_r exp(i q·r) n†_{rs}, and similarly for p†. The one-particle basis therefore has four spin/flavor choices at each allowed momentum.

For a zero-total-momentum spin singlet, choose a momentum q and its opposite −q. Writing the states explicitly in the neutron/proton basis gives

|nn;q,S=0⟩ = [n†_{q↑} n†_{−q↓} − n†_{q↓} n†_{−q↑}]|0⟩/√2,
|pp;q,S=0⟩ = [p†_{q↑} p†_{−q↓} − p†_{q↓} p†_{−q↑}]|0⟩/√2,
|np;q,S=0⟩ = [n†_{q↑} p†_{−q↓} − n†_{q↓} p†_{−q↑}]|0⟩/√2.

The np expression uses the ordering neutron first, proton second. For identical nn or pp particles these expressions are normalized as written for q ≠ 0; at q = 0 the normalized state is simply n†_{0↑}n†_{0↓}|0⟩ or p†_{0↑}p†_{0↓}|0⟩. The spin-singlet spin wavefunction is antisymmetric, so the spatial part for identical particles is symmetric, as required by fermionic antisymmetry.

(b) Fourier transformation of the kinetic term gives the free lattice dispersion

ε(q) = 2t Σ_{i=x,y,z} [1 − cos(q_i)].

The lowest nonzero lattice momentum has one component equal to 2π/L and the other two zero, so its energy is ε_1 = 2t[1 − cos(2π/L)]. In the physical periodic box, the corresponding continuum momentum is p_1 = 2π/L_phy, and its nonrelativistic energy is E_1 = (2π/L_phy)^2/(2M_phy), in units with ℏ = c = 1. Equating these energies gives the exact finite-L matching result

t = (2π/L_phy)^2 / {4 M_phy [1 − cos(2π/L)]}.

With a = L_phy/L, expanding for large L gives t → 1/(2 M_phy a²), the continuum-limit hopping parameter. The exact expression above applies to the stated matching of the first nonzero modes; the expansion is its small-spacing limit.

(c) By that matching, the lowest nonzero single-particle energy is the continuum box energy. Restoring ℏc to use fm and MeV,

E_1 = [2π(197.32698 MeV·fm)/3.4 fm]^2 / [2(1634 MeV)] ≈ 40.7 MeV.

(d)–(e) As stated, these parts do not determine a numerical bare C or discrete first and second excited-state energies. The issue is that the thermodynamic limit and continuum limit are different: L → ∞ at fixed a makes the physical volume La grow, whereas a → 0 at fixed L_phy is a continuum limit in a box of fixed physical size. Neither limit, by itself, specifies the missing regulator/volume information needed for the requested discrete spectrum.

For example, on the specified lattice let g = Ct, take a zero-total-momentum pair, and write its bound-state energy as E = −B, with B = 17.8 MeV. The two-body contact-interaction condition is

1/|g| = (1/L³) Σ_q 1/[B + 2ε(q)].

In the infinite-lattice-volume limit at fixed lattice spacing this becomes

1/|Ct| = ∫_[−π,π]³ d³q/(2π)³ · 1/{B + 4t Σ_i[1 − cos(q_i)]}.

This equation could determine C once the lattice spacing (and hence t and the ultraviolet cutoff) is specified. The bare dimensionless C depends on that cutoff; the supplied binding energy alone does not fix it as a regulator-independent number. In a zero-range continuum description, B instead fixes a physical scattering length under the zero-range assumption: B = 1/(M_phy a_s²), giving a_s ≈ 197.327/√(1634·17.8) fm ≈ 1.16 fm. That physical result is not a value for the bare lattice C.

In infinite volume the spectrum consists of the bound state at −17.8 MeV and a scattering continuum starting at E = 0 (energies measured relative to two particles at rest). The threshold E = 0 is not a discrete excited eigenstate, so there is no discrete first or second excited state, nor a finite degeneracy for a second excited level, in the stated thermodynamic limit. If instead a finite periodic box was intended, its physical size and a finite-volume prescription must be specified; its interacting levels and degeneracies would then be a different, discrete-spectrum problem.
